In this paper, we introduce the concept of the trimmed metric dimension of a graph, which is the minimum cardinality of a subset of vertices such that every vertex in the graph is uniquely determined by its distances to the vertices in the subset, except for a specified set of vertices. We study the properties of the trimmed metric dimension and provide upper and lower bounds for it. We also investigate the relationship between the trimmed metric dimension and other graph parameters, such as the metric dimension and the domination number. Finally, we present some examples and applications of the trimmed metric dimension in various fields, such as network design and sensor placement.

The peeling of an adhesive tape is a ubiquitous process that is often accompanied by crackling noise. This noise is generated by the stick-slip motion of the tape as it is peeled off a surface. We find that the crackling noise is composed of a series of discrete events that are separated by periods of silence. The discrete events are characterized by a power-law distribution of their amplitudes. The power-law distribution suggests that the discrete events are generated by a self-organized criticality process. We also find that the discrete events are correlated with the stick-slip motion of the tape. The correlation suggests that the discrete events are generated by the stick-slip motion. Our results provide new insights into the physical processes that are responsible for the crackling noise during the peeling of an adhesive tape.

Overall, our work presents a promising approach to enhancing the quality of point cloud models, which has the potential to impact a wide range of applications in computer vision and robotics.

Federated learning (FL) is a distributed machine learning paradigm that enables collaborative model training across multiple clients without sharing raw data. However, the heterogeneity of data across clients poses a significant challenge to the performance of FL. In this paper, we propose a novel approach to address this issue by leveraging the concept of random walks. Our method, called Stroll for Learning, involves constructing a graph where nodes represent clients and edges represent the similarity between their data distributions. By performing random walks on this graph, we can identify clusters of clients with similar data distributions and train separate models for each cluster. This approach not only improves the accuracy of the global model but also reduces the communication overhead and training time. We evaluate our method on several real-world datasets and demonstrate its effectiveness in improving the performance of FL in the presence of data heterogeneity.

However, the performance of deep learning models can be affected by the presence of outlier samples in the training data. In this paper, we propose a method for detecting outlier samples in the training data using entropy. We also propose a method for improving the performance of deep learning models by removing the outlier samples from the training data. Our method is evaluated on a dataset of skin cancer images and shows promising results.

The paper titled "Inverse Challenge for a Structural Acoustic Interaction" presents a method for solving the inverse problem in structural-acoustic interaction. The method involves using a finite element model to simulate the interaction between a structure and its surrounding acoustic environment. The inverse problem is then solved by adjusting the model parameters to match the observed data.
